transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Head of ML Ops - Polaris), Sofia Martinez (Platform Engineer), Liam Chen (CTO)

Summary (auto): quick POC scoping to capture QPS, concurrency, token distribution, success criteria, timelines and benchmarks. Agreed next steps to exchange logs, run baseline benchmarks, and follow up with pricing and deployment recommendations.

Topics: workload characterization, QPS & concurrency targets, input/output token distributions, lat/ cost tradeoffs, security concerns for POC, baseline benchmark plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everybody thanks for joining, um let’s do quick intros — jordan from redwood, maya se on the team, and from polaris?
[00:10] Evan: yeah hi i’m evan, head of ml ops at polaris, we have sofi and liam here too.
[00:15] Sofia: hey everyone
[00:17] Liam: hi all
[00:22] Jordan: cool, purpose of the call is a poc scoping for your claims automation use case — we want to capture qps, concurrency, token distributions and what success looks like for you. should take ~45.
[00:35] Maya: i’ll dig into the technical questions and benchmark framing, jordan will cover commercial and next steps.
[00:42] Evan: perfect. high level — we want an ml-driven assistant to triage incoming claims, extract entities, summarize long descriptions, and suggest severity. main constraint is latency for interactive use by our agents — aiming sub 300ms 90th, but we can discuss tradeoffs.
[01:05] Jordan: sub 300 90th for a live agent flow is pretty ambitious but feasible with the right model and dedicated infra; curious what your current traffic looks like?
[01:16] Evan: currently about 20 qps peak across our US region, typical concurrency for the agent UI is ~35 concurrent sessions during the morning spike. backlog batch jobs run off-hours.
[01:30] Sofia: also note payload sizes vary — short descriptions 50-80 tokens, long attachments parsed into text slices often 600-1,200 tokens. average input across all requests is around 220 tokens.
[01:45] Maya: that’s super helpful. can you confirm output sizes — are you returning full summaries or structured fields?
[01:52] Evan: we return a structured JSON with extracted fields (small) plus a 2-3 sentence plain-text summary, so output distribution is often 50-150 tokens, with occasional 400 token outputs for long-form summaries.
[02:10] Jordan: okay so input median ~220, outputs median ~90, with long-tail to 1200. what about model quality expectations — hallucination budget, deterministic outputs?
[02:22] Liam: quality is paramount — we need <5% critical extraction errors on entity fields and summaries must not hallucinate facts from PII. We’ll add post-hoc validation but model must be good enough.
[02:35] Maya: noted. for the poc we typically run head-to-head benchmarks on 1) accuracy/precision on extraction tasks 2) latency P90/P99 under target concurrency 3) cost-per-1000-requests and 4) stability under bursty traffic.
[02:52] Evan: that aligns with our criteria. timeline wise, we want a 6-week POC: week 1 scoping and data handoff, week 2 baseline benchmarks, weeks 3-4 optimization (batching/quantization/dedicated sizing), week 5 production-like run, week 6 decision and pricing review.
[03:12] Jordan: 6 weeks is realistic. for dedicated we’ll need to size gpu pool — with your numbers (20 qps peak, 35 concurrency, median tokens) we can sketch starting references.
[03:25] Maya: quick modeling — if median input+output = ~310 tokens, and we target 20 qps sustained with 35 concurrency, the key is per-token throughput and context window. what model family are you considering?
[03:40] Evan: we’re open, we have internal preference for open models due to licensing — we've looked at Llama-3 style variants and some llama-x quantized builds, but we’re open to redwood suggestions.
[03:52] Jordan: got it. competitor note: you mentioned anthropic/oa earlier — fine. for modeling let’s show two scenarios: hosted (managed, autoscaling) and dedicated (reserved gpus). maya — can you walk through a quick compute estimate?
[04:05] Maya: sure. assumption A: using a 8-bit quantized 13b variant, token throughput on an A100-ish GPU is ~1,200 tokens/sec for generation under typical configs (this is a rough / depends on kernel selection). Inference is mostly generation for summaries; extraction often uses shorter prompts and can be faster.
[04:28] Maya: math: 310 tokens per request * 20 qps = 6,200 tokens/sec. at 1,200 tokens/sec per gpu that equals ~5.2 GPUs sustained; factor in burst and overhead so start with 8 GPUs for dedicated baseline.
[04:44] Sofia: that’s useful. what about latency targets — sub 300ms P90 seems tricky if many requests hit 1,200 token generation.
[04:54] Maya: right — 1,200 tokens/sec implies ~0.26s per 310-token response on average purely on generation time, but that excludes tokenization, decode overhead, network, batching delays. With optimized kernels and continuous batching we can get close but P90 will depend on batching policy and whether you accept slightly smaller models or more GPUs.
[05:15] Jordan: tradeoff examples: smaller model (7b quantized) could give sub-300 P90 with lower quality; dedicated scaling to 12 GPUs reduces per-gpu load and latency but increases cost. We’ll include cost examples in the deck.
[05:33] Evan: curious about batching — do you recommend aggressive batching to improve throughput or prefer per-request low latency?
[05:41] Maya: Redwood supports workload-aware batching and prefix caching. For interactive agent flows, we prefer small batch windows (<20ms) to keep latency low, and enable caching for repeated prompts. For background batch jobs, larger batching helps cost.
[05:55] Liam: we also need KV cache and long context support for multi-message conversations — typical agent session will send prior 2-3 messages (context ~500 tokens). how does that impact memory and GPU selection?
[06:07] Maya: longer context increases memory; quantized 13b with 2k context is fine on A100 80GB but pushing to 8k context or multiple concurrent sessions with large context needs more memory headroom. We’ll capture context distribution in the logs.
[06:23] Evan: ok we’ll include context lengths in the export.
[06:27] Jordan: security questions — polaris will likely require SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration for private deployments. is redwood private an option?
[06:36] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs. for the poc we can start hosted or dedicated in a customer VPC depending on compliance needs — we’ll surface differences in the proposal.
[06:50] Sofia: audit log retention and data residency are important — EU data residency for some customers. we’ll flag requirements after we review security docs.
[06:58] Jordan: we’ll send the security pack and SOC2 artifact.
[07:02] Evan: cool. back to benchmarks — what does the baseline test look like?
[07:07] Maya: baseline: 1) single-GPU baseline with quantized 13b to measure per-request latency, throughput given your sample payloads; 2) 8-gpu dedicated sim to estimate P90/P99 under 20 qps with real traffic shape (bursts); 3) model quality eval on your labeled prompt set for extraction tasks. We’ll run stress tests with synthetic bursts to ensure graceful degradation.
[07:33] Jordan: what data do you need from us for realistic runs?
[07:36] Evan: 48 hours of request logs (timestamps, payload sizes, token counts, endpoints), a representative labeled eval set for extraction accuracy (~500 examples), sample requests for long narratives, and details on SLOs.
[07:51] Maya: perfect. please remove PII before upload, we can handle anonymized payloads. we’ll provide a csv template.
[07:59] Sofia: quick question on cost metrics — how will you report cost-per-1000-requests?
[08:04] Jordan: we’ll produce cost breakdown by per-token compute, GPU hourly amortization, and infra overhead. for hosted we’ll show a per-1k estimate; for dedicated we’ll show monthly GPU cost and per-request amortized.
[08:18] Liam: any guardrails for hallucination or deterministic behavior?
[08:22] Maya: can use system prompts, constrained generation, and n-best scoring with reranking. also recommend a small validation pipeline to check extracted entities against authoritative fields.
[08:35] Evan: about throughput modeling — can you show an example traffic shape?
[08:39] Maya: yes — we model qps as baseline sustained 10 qps with 20 qps peak sustained for 10 minute windows and microbursts up to 60 qps for 30s. concurrency map shows 35 concurrent interactive sessions at peak, plus background batch processes. we’ll include a spreadsheet with percentile token sizes.
[09:00] Jordan: fantastic. on success criteria what will you accept?
[09:04] Liam: success = meet P90 latency <= 350ms (we can compromise from 300), extraction accuracy >= 95% on labeled set, and cost below our threshold (tbd after pricing). Also no major security blockers for the deployment model.
[09:20] Jordan: we’ll aim for P90 <= 350ms in proposal.
[09:24] Evan: any red flags about the numbers we gave?
[09:27] Maya: nothing impossible — the long-tail 1,200 token requests drive GPU needs; we might suggest a hybrid pattern: route long summaries to an async path with higher latency, keep interactive path limited to 300-400 tokens using extract+concise summary templates.
[09:45] Sofia: that’s a good idea — we can change agent UI to request async full summaries for heavy cases.
[09:50] Jordan: great. next steps recap: jordan sends pricing and deployment comparison, maya shares workload template and benchmark scripts, polaris provides logs and labeled eval. schedule baseline run week of 4/20.
[10:05] Evan: agreed. timeline OK.
[10:08] Liam: quick legal curiosity — do you have an NDA for the logs?
[10:12] Jordan: yes we have an NDA and we can sign a data processing addendum; i’ll attach links.
[10:18] Sofia: thanks. one more: for private deployment what's the lead time to provision?
[10:22] Maya: private on-prem lead time depends on procurement but typical 6-8 weeks; VPC/private cloud can be faster ~2-3 weeks if credentials are ready. we’ll outline that.
[10:34] Evan: ok good.
[10:36] Jordan: anything else?
[10:38] Sofia: not from me.
[10:40] Liam: no
[10:42] Jordan: ok we’ll follow-up with the artifacts. thanks everyone.
[10:46] (end)
